title.narrative: SGBV Response and Mitigation in Somalia

description.narrative:
Prolonged and recurring conflict across the Horn of Africa and the Sahel has resulted in dire humanitarian needs and forced millions of people to flee their homes, adopt negative coping mechanisms, and increased exposure to a multitude of risks. The disputed regions of Sool and Sanaag face ongoing cyclical humanitarian crises, armed conflict, drought and flooding. It is estimated up to 203,000 people are living in IDP settlements in Las Anood district or neighbouring districts including Buhoodle in Togdheer. Despite fighting ending, the situation remains very tense with high humanitarian needs among both displaced and host communities. Protection monitoring mechanisms found an upward trend of SGBV, particularly IPV and assault.[6] Oxfam’s 2023 GPA found that rape was the biggestprotection concern reported by women (59%) and girls (55.4%). Conflict has compounded the impacts of a drought ongoing since 2017 and 43% of people (214,000) in Sool and Togdheer regions are in IPC 3 ‘Crisis’ (including most IDP settlements) and IPC 4 ’Emergency’(including IDP and urban populations of Las Anood). Oxfam’s 2023 IRNA found widespread household income vulnerability, with 60% of HH experiencing declining income, 58% of HHs spending more than half of their income onfood and 18% on water.
Oxfam’s work is guided by its Gender in Emergencies Strategy (2022–2025) and Gender Standards (2022) and grounded in feminist theory and practice. These frame an effective, holistic and comprehensive approach to humanitarian action that acknowledges and addresses gender in a responsive, appropriate, and equitable manner. Oxfam’s global experience and expertise leading SGBV, SRH and GiE programming makes it well placed to respond to the increased risk of SGBV in humanitarian contexts and deliver life-saving SRH information and services. Oxfam staff and partners mainstream gender through its WASH and Protection work, as well as gender-targeted action, which includes SRH, SGBV risk mitigation, prevention and response and women’s leadership. Oxfam has a large global portfolio of programming, including ongoing programming in the proposed target communities that aims to address gender inequality and the gendered impacts of humanitarian crises. Oxfam, together with six local implementing partners, propose to implement a multi-country, multi-sectorial, survivor-centredapproach to respond to the intersectional SRH, SGBV and protection needs identified by SGBV survivors, while also mitigating SGBV exposure through community-based protection mechanisms, rehabilitation and provision of critical WASH infrastructure and hygiene items.
Oxfam will work with partners, APLFT, We-Action, Mums for Mums, KAALO, ATAD and UNIJED who have extensive experience implementing humanitarian programming,including SGBV and protection work. The program will contribute towards reduced suffering, increased protection and lives saved of women, men, boys and girls, especially SGBV survivors, in targeted conflict and crisis-affected communities in South Sudan,Somalia, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso and Chad over 24 months. The proposed intervention is aligned with the CERF Lifesaving Criteria, Inter-Agency Minimum Standards for Gender-Based Violence in Emergencies Programming, Inter-Agency Field Manual on Reproductive Health in Humanitarian Settings, WHO’s Clinical Management of Rape and Intimate Partner Violence Survivors: Developing Protocols for Use in Humanitarian Settings, IASC Guidelines for Integrating Gender-based Violence Interventions in Humanitarian Action and the Humanitarian Response Plans (HRP) in all five countries.
The target communities are IPC level 3, 4 and 5, in areas with high reported levels of SGBV, recurring or recently ended conflict, and facing multiple other crises including drought andnear-famine like conditions. Oxfam and partners will prioritize communities with large displaced populations and limited access to infrastructureand resources to meet their basic needs. Across the targeted communities, Oxfam plans to reach approximately242,962 individuals, including 88,592 women, 59,503 men, 52,092 girls and 42,775 boys, 10% of whom will be people living with disabilities (PLWDs). An estimated 70% of people assisted will come from out-of-camp IDP populations and the remaining 30% from the host community.
The UltimateOutcome of the program is reduced suffering, increased protection and lives saved of women, men, boys and girls, especially SGBV survivors, in conflict-affected target communities in South Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso and Chad. Oxfam will achieve this goal by responding to identified SRH and SGBV needs, while mitigating SGBV exposure through strengthening community-based protection mechanisms, and rehabilitation of critical WASH infrastructure and hygiene items.
The transition, exit and sustainability of gains has been considered throughout the design of this program. Community members, community leaders and local and technical authorities will be supported by Oxfam and partners to draw up exit plans at theoutset. These will include a reflection on the achievements of the program and identification of key activities to be carried out beyond the program life. The exit strategy in each context will bebased on several integrated mechanisms.

participating-org.narrative:
KAALO Aid and Development is a non-profit humanitarian and development organization established in Somalia in 1991 just after the collapse of the central government. KAALO works in Nugal, Mudug, Bari, Sool, Sanaag and Karkaar regions and plans to expand services to cover more regions of Somalia.
KAALO#s vision is a #Society free of ignorance and poverty# and its mission is to improve the livelihoods of communities in Somalia by supporting the provision of basic needs in a sustainable and environmentally sound manner. Currently the key program areas for KAALO are education and research, democracy, human rights, governance and rule of law, livelihood and community empowerment, agriculture and rural infrastructure, health water and sanitation. Current funding partners for KAALO include UNHCR, UNHABITAT, National Endowment for Democracy (NED), Diakonia, Danish People#s Aid (DPA), Oxfam Novib and Caritas International Belgium.
KAALO has been in partnership with Oxfam since 2006. They were an implementing partner with Oxfam Novib for several long term development projects among them the Human rights program #2006-2008# which was funded by the EC, they are also currently implementing on two big projects both funded by the EC: #Strengthening capacity of civil society organisations to provide life skills and vocational training for the youth# and #Support to Artisanal Fisheries and Coastal Management in Somaliland and Puntland#
KAALOhas registered the following key achievements to date:
# Undertook the largest program that a Civil Society Organization implemented in Puntland. This involved distribution of about 60 tonnes of books, journals, hospital beds, other hospital equipments, wheelchairs, crutches e.t.c. to Somali communities across Somalia in 2001. Counterpart International in Washington USA contributed the shipment. # Carried out the first public building relocation program since the collapse of the last Central government in 1993 - 94 in Nugal region of Somalia. # Established the first professional training institute, Garowe School of Management, in Puntland in 1999. Renamed Puntland Community College in 2001 and grew to become Puntland State University in 2004. # Implemented the first Puntland administration funded community project (Drought Relief Program) during the 2003 # 04 drought in Puntland. # Developed human rights curriculum and a HIV/AIDS curriculum and had them integrated in the Puntland State University curriculum.
